messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: pD for DIC
parts:
Hi all

I have a doubt related to how to calculate properly the DIC. In BDA 3 in page 172 - 173 explains the calculation of the dice, which includes the deviance and the pD (the effective number of parameters). My concern is about the pD. BDA mentions 2 ways to calculate it, the first is how i have seen it in many articles, the second one BDA explains it is also valid but it doesnt explain it extensively.

The first one is
pD = Dbar -  Dhat

The second one is
pDalt = 2 variance(log-likelihood)

Could someone help me understand the similarities between these 2 calculations and the differences? Or guide to a articles that exaplains it more extensively (since i havent been able to find one)?

I also found that jags gives the first method mentioned here and a third method propose by Martyn Plummer (Penalized loss functions for Bayesian model comparison, 2008), and these can be obtain using the r package rjags, but using the package R2jags, it only gives the DIC using the pDalt.

Given that there are other information criteria that are based on the deviance, and the difference is in the penalized (pD), like AIC and BIC, using different pD's to calculate the DIC would give three different DIC's, and these three DIC's should not be consider the same, but different information criteria?

Thanks for any help

 - Mauricio

messages.author: 20758fda448fdbda
messages.subject: Re: pD for DIC
parts:
If you have Andrew's BDA3, you'll see that he has been moving away from DIC and promoting WAIC in its stead. WAIC does require capturing the likelihood at each data point for the simulations, but it then allows you to calculate the expected value of each data points likelihood over the space of the simulated parameters, which is a Bayesian measure, as opposed to DIC which substitutes the expected likelihood at the posterior mean of the parameters.

Here is a very simple model among those I am using to give you an idea. Stan file first capturing the likelihoods at each data point:

data {
  int<lower = 0> N;
  vector<lower = 0.0>[N] Y;
}
parameters {
  real mu;  // prior for mu
  real<lower = 0.0> sigma;  // non-negative prior for sigma
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(0.0, 10.0);
  sigma ~ uniform(0.0, 100.0);
  Y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);          
}
generated quantities {
  real Y_posterior;
  vector[N] PointLikelihoods;  // log pointwise predictive density
  for (i in 1:N) {
    PointLikelihoods[i] <- exp(lognormal_log(Y[i], mu, sigma));
  }
  Y_posterior <- lognormal_rng(mu, sigma);  // stochastic observation of Y
}

If "A" is your stanfit object, and A_E is extract(A), then there will be an A_E$PointLikelihoods matrix which contains the observations of the likelihood at each point for each parameter set captured by Stan. Now you can calculate the WAIC in R by using:

WAIC <- function(pointMatrix) {
# Using the definition of population variance E(X^2) - E(X)^2, colMeans, and the bias correction was faster than using apply and FUN = var.  
  lppd <- sum(log(colMeans(pointMatrix)))
  LogMatrix <- log(pointMatrix)
  n <- dim(LogMatrix)[1]
  pWAIC2 <- sum((colMeans(LogMatrix^2) - colMeans(LogMatrix)^2)) * n / (n - 1)
  return(-2 * (lppd - pWAIC2))
}Enter code here...

If you still want DIC, you will have to calculate the deviance in the generated parameter section and it will then be easier to use DIC = mean(deviance) + 1/2 * var(deviance).

Hope that helps!

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] pD for DIC
parts:
The information criteria aren’t independent — they actually follow a pretty rigid criteria,

evidence -> BIC

cross validation -> WAIC -> DIC -> AIC

where “->” denotes further approximations.  So WAIC and DIC don’t have different approximations
in as much as DIC has more approximations than WAIC.

For more see http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ssu/1356628931 and http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf.
